collection.credit:
NEW EVENTS — DISABILITY AND HUMAN DIVERSITY (DIV-01..50, draft for the owner, 2026-11-15)
Disabled villagers, chronic illness and every kind of body, skin, hair and face: wheelchairs with real wheels, crutches, canes, ear trumpets, signs and lenses made from island materials; good days and hard days; competence, humor and opinions. Sometimes the difference is the story. Often it's just part of the scenery.
Written in the style of the owner's own events. Edit anything and send it back; nothing ships until you approve.

ledger.why: the casting line, carried out as the roles' ages (picks a child aged 6-13 and another child; in the story (name1)'s eyes point in slightly different directions)

collection.description: A younger child asks which of a child's eyes to look at, since one drifts outward: answer back, or ignore it and keep playing.

setup.name: The setup
setup.text: (subject)'s eyes don't point quite the same way; one tends to drift a little outward. It's always been like that. Today a younger child, (friend), squints at (subject.him/her) and says, "You're looking at me funny. Which eye do I look at?"

o1.name: Outcome A
o1.text: "Either," says (subject). "I'm looking at you with this one and the parrot behind you with the other." (friend) spins round. There is, in fact, a parrot. (friend) is deeply impressed. For the rest of the day (friend.he/she) follows (subject) around asking what (subject.his/her) other eye is looking at. Most of the answers are made up. Some of them aren't.

o2.name: Outcome B
o2.text: (subject) has heard it a hundred times and doesn't feel like answering. "Do you want to play or not?" (subject.he/she) says. (friend) does. They play crabs-and-fishers until dark, and (friend) never asks again. Later, at home, (friend) tells (friend.his/her) family about (subject)'s amazing fish-catching technique. It doesn't occur to (friend.him/her) to mention the eyes.
